summary:
Şırnak province yields no trans-specific statute, enforcement series or documented incident in the available sources, and none of the monitoring reports used here breaks its figures down by province. The assessment therefore rests on the national framework of Turkey, which applies within the province, and on the identity-document and checkpoint rules that bind foreign visitors there.

A leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, was reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. It would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, behind mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft; Human Rights Watch warned that its provisions would force treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest.

Kaos GL's 2025 review, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people has become explicit state policy. Public institutions received "Year of the Family" instructions, an LGBTI+ rights organisation was closed for the first time in years, expression and artistic freedom were restricted, and events were cancelled or banned.

The same review records 6 right-to-life violations, of which 3 were hate-motivated killings, with transgender people the most affected. Torture and ill-treatment violations rose to 89 from 51 the prior year. Liberty violations reached 313, about two and a half times the previous year's total, including 299 detention decisions. Private-life violations rose from 16 to 67, among them obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy, and 61 travel bans were imposed.

Foreign nationals are required to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents are compared against presentation, creating a direct outing risk where appearance does not match the passport gender marker.
tangentialFactors:
The national numbers are directional rather than provincial: no source consulted reports violation counts, detentions or bans attributable to Şırnak, so the province's picture is an inference from country-wide monitoring rather than a measurement.

Street-level enforcement documented in Istanbul shows how the national posture operates in practice. In 2025 police stopped roughly 20 trans women in Beyoğlu district, in streets, shops and cafés, and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release, without fines but with the women documented. One detainee observed that the pending law had not been passed even as its terms were already being applied to her. Foreign visitors stopped at such checkpoints must produce original identity documents.

The 61 travel bans recorded nationally bear directly on mobility, and the pending draft's proposed penalties for healthcare providers and patients would sit alongside existing checkpoint practice rather than replace it.
localsOnly:
Turkish residents live under the monitoring picture Kaos GL describes: 313 liberty violations in 2025 with 299 detention decisions, 89 torture and ill-treatment violations against 51 the year before, and private-life violations rising from 16 to 67. Obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy is recorded within that private-life category.

Public institutions operate under "Year of the Family" instructions, expression and artistic freedom are restricted, and events have been cancelled or banned. One LGBTI+ rights organisation was closed, the first such closure in years.

Trans prisoners are placed according to registered sex, and LGBT detainees are held under segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement, with reports of arbitrary body and strip searches, restricted healthcare access and ineffective complaints procedures.

Transition-related care is administered through medical boards: a Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted remains unresolved in the sources available; Human Rights Watch reported it as a leaked draft on 29 October 2025 and no later source in the inventory confirms its status. Its terms are therefore described as proposed, not in force.

No source consulted documents trans-specific enforcement, pride activity, healthcare access or incidents of violence within Şırnak province itself. Local police practice in the province, the presence or absence of any LGBTI+ organisation there, and the treatment of detainees by Şırnak authorities are not sourced and are left open.

The province-level application of the national monitoring figures is not stated by Kaos GL or Human Rights Watch, which report country-wide totals; attributing any share of the 313 liberty violations or 299 detentions to Şırnak would be unsupported.
